implementation_notes: C++17's std::variant is the standard library's type-safe discriminated union: it stores the active alternative in place, never holds two, and owns a generated index that plays the role of the tag. std::visit applies a callable to whichever alternative is active, std::holds_alternative/std::get_if test or extract it, and index() exposes the discriminant. Prefer it to a raw union whenever payloads have non-trivial copy/destructors, where the enclosing type would need hand-written special member functions. Keep the alternative list small and closed; if the set must stay open for extension, a polymorphic hierarchy is the right tool instead.
pitfalls: A variant can become valueless_by_exception() when an alternative's constructor throws during type-changing assignment; visit then throws bad_variant_access.
Overload resolution in std::visit needs exactly one viable overload per alternative - a generic lambda can silently swallow cases you meant to be exhaustive.
Alternatives are matched by exact type: a variant<int, std::string> does not accept const char* without conversion, which surprises C-style callers.

variants.name: Hand-rolled tag enum + raw union (pre-C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++17 (or where a project pins C++03/11), the tagged union is written the same way as in C: an enumerator for the discriminant plus a raw union, with an accessor that switches on the tag. Constructors that set both fields consistently are the only safeguard, since the union cannot record which member is live. Choose this only to avoid the standard library version or to keep POD-only layouts; otherwise std::variant gives the same in-place representation with a checked tag.
pitfalls: In C++03 a union may only hold members without user-provided constructors/destructors; from C++11 non-trivial members are allowed but the enclosing type's special member functions are deleted unless written by hand.
Reading the member that is not the active one is undefined behaviour - the tag does not prevent it.
Padding and alignment make the union as large as its largest member; a tagged union of big payloads should store them indirectly.
